title: Guarded methods in OCaml
excerpt: Implementation of "guarded methods" using type equality witnesses
content_html:
Guarded methods make it possible to attach constraints to the receiver (self) only for certain methods, meaning these methods can only be called if the receiver satisfies those constraints (these guards). OCaml does not, syntactically, allow defining this kind of method directly. In this note, we’ll look at how to encode them using a type equality witness.

Problem presentation

When a language (where type checking is done before the program runs, like in Java or OCaml) introduces parametric polymorphism (Java's generics), it's sometimes possible to constrain type variables. For example:

class MyClass<T extends S> { ... }

We make MyClass generic by assuming that the type variable T is a subtype of S. The problem is that the constraint applies to the entire class. Yet sometimes, we’d like to have constraints apply only to certain methods. For example, let’s say we have a class MyList describing a list:

class MyList<A> extends ArrayList<A> {
   public int length() {
     return this.size();
   }
}

How can we define a flatten method that, for a list like [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5]], would produce the list [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]? If we place the constraint at the class level, we force our list to be "always a list of lists," which is very limiting. To implement such a method, we have three theoretical approaches available.

Moving the method outside the class

The first solution is the most obvious: simply "cheat" by moving the method outside the class body (for example, into the static context or a companion object):

class MyList<A> extends ArrayList<A> {
   public static <A> MyList<A> flatten(MyList<MyList<A>> list) {
      // Flatten's implementation
   }
   public int length() {
     return this.size();
   }
}

This approach works and doesn’t require any special ceremony. However, it forces the developer to keep track of which methods are in the class body and which are in the static context. Moreover, it breaks the systematic approach of sending messages to an instance (often presented as one of the key arguments in favor of object-oriented programming).

Extension methods

Kotlin (and others, like C#) offer extension methods which, in addition to allowing the extension of an already existing class (which can be very useful for adding behavior to the String class, which is final in Java), also provide more flexibility in defining the receiver. For example, we could write flatten like this (in Kotlin):

class MyList<A> : ArrayList<A> { ... }
fun <A> MyList<MyList<A>>.flatten() = ...

Even though this solution seems nearly perfect, it still requires the method to be defined outside the class, which might potentially mean having to make certain members of the class public in order to be accessible from an extension (looks like potentials leaky abstractions). However, it still preserves the systematic message-sending approach while allowing for more fine-grained qualification of the receiver.

Guarded methods

The final approach is probably the most ideological, as it keeps the method definition within the class. It doesn't force any escaped abstractions. This is the idea of guarded methods, the ability to add constraints on the generic parameter at the method definition level. In an imaginary syntax (this code compiles because it's not syntactically invalid, but it doesn’t produce the intended effect):

class MyList<A> : ArrayList<A>() {
    fun length() = size
    fun <B> MyList<MyList<B>>.flatten() =
        // Implémentation de flatten
}

Even though this doesn’t seem significantly different from classic extension methods (as evidenced by their syntax, which inside the class body seems sufficient), it addresses all the issues raised earlier:

  • we can characterize the receiver more precisely than in a normal method
  • we don’t break the regular message sending
  • we still benefit from available members (so we don’t escape representations)

Although guarded methods seem necessary, unfortunately, I don’t know of any mainstream languages that allow their definition. That’s very sad. Fortunately, in OCaml, it is possible to encode them.

OOP/FP symmetry: theory and practice

Since guarded methods are quite rare in popular programming languages, I discovered their existence fairly recently while reading the slides from the presentation "The Object-Oriented/Functional-Programming symmetry: theory and practice" by Gabriel Scherer.

I recommend this presentation, which showcases a symmetry between the tools of statically typed functional programming and object-oriented programming. Even though this symmetry has been observed and studied many times, the presentation is comprehensive and accessible (and relatively unbiased, discussing the pros and cons of both approaches). Unfortunately not covered during the presentation (time is often the enemy of a presenter), an entire section on guarded methods is included in the slides. The original example offers a symmetrical observation between the implementation of the flatten function in a classic functional style:

type 'a list = ...
let rec length : 'a list -> int = ...
let rec concat : 'a list -> 'a list -> 'a list = ...

let rec flatten : 'a list list -> 'a list = function
  | [] -> []
  | x::xs -> x @ flatten xs

And the implementation of a flatten method if we were in the object-oriented world, posing exactly the problem introduced in this note. The question is: what type should flatten have?

class type ['a] olist = object
  method length : int
  method concat : 'a olist -> 'a olist

  method flatten : ???
end

He therefore proposes this syntax, which implies a guard on the flatten method:

method flatten : 'b olist with 'a = 'b olist

This syntax allows describing a guarded method and could be generalized like this: method method_name : return_type with generic_type = other_type. Similar to substitutions in modules, we could specify constraints on multiple generics using and. For example: method foo : string with 'a = string and b = int for a class parameterized by two types: class ['a, 'b] t.

Additionally, this syntax would also allow defining specific behaviors elegantly. For example, for our olist type, we could provide a sum method if the elements of the list are integers:

class type ['a] olist = object
  method length : int
  method concat : 'a olist -> 'a olist
  method flatten : 'b olist with 'a = 'b olist
  method sum : int with 'a = int
end

All of this sounds extraordinary, but unfortunately, this syntax is not available in OCaml. That’s annoying! Don’t worry, it is possible to encode it using a few small tools.

Guarded methods in OCaml

Even though I had a fairly clear idea of the tools to use for encoding guarded methods, after running into a few corner cases, I decided to call on someone in the OCaml community who never asks questions but always answers them expansively: Florian Angeletti, also known as Octachron. (A fun little note: octachron is the name of a MIDI drum sequencer, so when I searched his nickname on Google, the suggestions immediately included octachron ocaml).

Our goal is to allow adding a constraint to certain methods so that they are only accessible if the receiver’s type satisfies it. Without modifying the language syntax, modeling a constraint can consist of providing an additional parameter that enforces it. In other words, we want to provide evidence.

Provide a type equality witness

Since the introduction of generalized algebraic data types in the language, there is a fairly straightforward way to define a type equality witness:

type (_, _) eq =
  | Refl : ('a, 'a) eq

The eq type, which has only one constructor: Refl, allows representing type equalities not known by the type-checker. Since we can only construct Refl values that associate two equal types, instantiating Refl within a scope guarantees that those types are equivalent. For example:

type other_int = int
let _ : (int, other_int) eq = Refl
(* Now, we have a proof of [int = other_int]. *)

This example is somewhat artificial because here the compiler knows perfectly well that int = other_int. However, there are cases where the compiler cannot know this. For example, when data is provided at runtime, where it makes perfect sense that the type-checker has no information about a type, or when the type’s representation is hidden by abstraction.

The goal of this note is not to delve into eq, so let’s just keep in mind that if we can construct a Refl value, we have a guarantee that two syntactically different types are actually equal.

Constrain with eq

Let’s return to our example that provides an object API for a list. Here is its interface:

class type ['a] obj_list =
  object ('self)
    method length : int
    method append : 'a list -> 'a obj_list
    method uncons : ('a * 'self) option
    method flatten : ???
  end

To give a type to flatten, we want to impose that 'a (the type parameter of the obj_list class) is a list. In other words, we want a proof that 'a is of type 'b list. That is, to guarantee that 'a and 'b list, though syntactically different, are equal. It’s simple: just require a value of type ('a, 'b list) eq to be provided:

method flatten : ('a, 'b list) eq -> 'b list

Now that we have an interface describing a list with a flatten method that constrains the receiver to be a list of something, let’s concretely implement a class that implements obj_list.

Implementing the interface obj_list

The first methods (length, append, and uncons) are straightforward to implement:

let my_list (list : 'a list) =
  object (self : 'a obj_list)
    val l = list
    method length = List.length l
    method append x = {<l = List.append l x>}
    method uncons = match l with [] -> None | x :: xs -> Some (x, {<l = xs>})

    method flatten = ???
  end

Now, let’s focus on flatten. We will recursively traverse the list, concatenating each element to the previous one. For example, [[1]; [2]; [3]] will become [1] @ [2]; [3]. Beyond the somewhat noisy annotations, the entire trick lies in instantiating Refl to provide evidence that 'a = 'b list.

method flatten : 'b. ('a, 'b list) eq -> 'b list =
  let rec aux : type a b. a #obj_list -> (a, b list) eq -> b list =
  fun list witness -> match list#uncons with
    | None -> []
    | Some (head_list, xs) ->
        let flatten_list : b list =
          let Refl = witness  in head_list
        in flatten_list @ aux xs witness
  in aux self

Adding a guarded method sum

Now that we’re able to constrain certain methods, let’s try adding a sum method that produces the sum of a list of integers! First, let’s add sum to our interface. This time, we want to constrain our type parameter to be int. To do that, we simply take ('a, int) eq as a type equality witness:

class type ['a] obj_list =
  object ('self)
    method length : int
    method append : 'a list -> 'a obj_list
    method uncons : ('a * 'self) option
    method flatten : ('a, 'b list) eq -> 'b list
    method sum : ('a, int) eq -> int
  end

Next, we can implement the sum method, which is just a use of the fold_left function.

method sum : ('a, int) eq -> int =
  let aux : type a. a list -> (a, int) eq -> int = fun list Refl ->
    List.fold_left (fun acc x -> acc + x) 0 list
  in aux l

The implementation of sum is logically simpler than that of flatten because it doesn’t introduce additional type variables. And we can test our different methods: we can invoke flatten on an object of type 'a list obj_list and sum on an object of type int obj_list.

let a = my_list [ [ 1 ]; [ 2 ]; [ 3 ] ]
let _ = assert ([ 1; 2; 3 ] = a#flatten Refl)
let b = my_list [ 1; 2; 3; 4 ]
let _ = assert (10 = b#sum Refl)

If we try to apply a guarded method with the wrong type, for example, trying to sum our list a (which is of type 'a list obj_list), the program will not compile. This makes sense, as we are trying to call a guarded method without respecting the imposed constraint.

1 | let _ = a#sum Refl
                  ^^^^
Error: This expression has type (int list, int list) eq
       but an expression was expected of type (int list, int) eq
       Type int list is not compatible with type int

Exactly the expected behavior! We can now define methods that constrain the receiver’s type by means of a type equality witness. Mission complete!

To conclude

It is surprising that guarded methods are not present in all statically typed OOP languages, since they allow expressing more methods while preserving the message-passing semantics so dear to object-oriented programming. Not being a heavy user of object-oriented programming languages (OCaml is the only one I use regularly), I’m not aware of languages offering syntactic support for guarded methods. However, I recently learned, pointed out by Nicolas Rinaudo, that the language Scala uses a similar encoding, but where the type equality witness is provided implicitly, thus lightening the call and not forcing the user to manually provide Refl.

Even though the encoding is somewhat heavy, and one could imagine native language support to simplify the definition of guarded methods, explicitly manipulating a type equality witness allows us to encode them. Is it useful? Since OOP programming is rarely encouraged in OCaml, probably not, but it was still fun to present a concrete and practical use case for equality witnesses!

blocks.html_en: It is surprising that guarded methods are not present in all statically typed OOP languages, since they allow expressing more methods while preserving the message-passing semantics so dear to object-oriented programming. Not being a heavy user of object-oriented programming languages (OCaml is the only one I use regularly), I’m not aware of languages offering syntactic support for guarded methods. However, I recently learned, pointed out by Nicolas Rinaudo, that the language Scala uses a similar encoding, but where the type equality witness is provided implicitly, thus lightening the call and not forcing the user to manually provide Refl.

content_html_zh:
受保护的方法可以仅针对某些方法向接收者（自身）附加约束，这意味着只有当接收者满足这些约束（这些保护）时才能调用这些方法。 从语法上来说，OCaml 不允许直接定义这种方法。 在本文中，我们将了解如何使用类型相等见证对它们进行编码。

问题呈现

当一种语言（在程序运行之前完成类型检查，例如 Java 或 OCaml）引入参数多态性（Java 的泛型）时，有时可以约束类型变量。 例如：

class MyClass<T extends S> { ... }

我们通过假设类型变量 T 是 S 的子类型来使 MyClass 成为泛型。 问题是该约束适用于整个类。 但有时，我们希望约束仅适用于某些方法。 例如，假设我们有一个描述列表的类 MyList：

class MyList<A> extends ArrayList<A> {
   public int length() {
     return this.size();
   }
}

我们如何定义一个扁平化方法，对于像 [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5]] 这样的列表，将生成列表 [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]？ 如果我们将约束放在类级别，我们就会强制我们的列表“始终是列表的列表”，这是非常有限的。 为了实现这种方法，我们可以使用三种理论方法。

将方法移到类之外

第一个解决方案是最明显的：通过将方法移到类主体之外（例如，移到静态上下文或伴随对象中）来简单地“作弊”：

class MyList<A> extends ArrayList<A> {
   public static <A> MyList<A> flatten(MyList<MyList<A>> list) {
      // Flatten's implementation
   }
   public int length() {
     return this.size();
   }
}

这种方法很有效，不需要任何特殊的仪式。 但是，它迫使开发人员跟踪哪些方法位于类主体中以及哪些方法位于静态上下文中。 此外，它打破了向实例发送消息的系统方法（通常被视为支持面向对象编程的关键论点之一）。

扩展方法

Kotlin（以及其他语言，如 C#）提供了扩展方法，除了允许扩展已存在的类（这对于向 String 类添加行为非常有用，在 Java 中为 Final 类）之外，还为定义接收器提供了更大的灵活性。 例如，我们可以像这样编写 flatten （在 Kotlin 中）：

class MyList<A> : ArrayList<A> { ... }
fun <A> MyList<MyList<A>>.flatten() = ...

尽管这个解决方案看起来近乎完美，但它仍然需要在类外部定义该方法，这可能意味着必须将类的某些成员公开才能从扩展访问（看起来可能存在泄漏抽象）。 然而，它仍然保留了系统的消息发送方法，同时允许对接收者进行更细粒度的限定。

受保护的方法

最后一种方法可能是最具意识形态性的，因为它将方法定义保留在类中。 它不会强制任何转义的抽象。 这就是受保护方法的思想，即在方法定义级别对泛型参数添加约束的能力。 在想象的语法中（此代码可以编译，因为它在语法上不是无效的，但它不会产生预期的效果）：

class MyList<A> : ArrayList<A>() {
    fun length() = size
    fun <B> MyList<MyList<B>>.flatten() =
        // Implémentation de flatten
}

尽管这看起来与经典扩展方法没有显着不同（从它们的语法可以看出，在类体内似乎就足够了），但它解决了之前提出的所有问题：

  • 我们可以比普通方法更精确地表征接收器
  • 我们不会破坏常规的消息发送
  • 我们仍然受益于可用的成员（所以我们不会逃避代表）

尽管受保护的方法似乎是必要的，但不幸的是，我不知道有任何主流语言允许它们的定义。 这非常令人难过。 幸运的是，在 OCaml 中，可以对它们进行编码。

OOP/FP 对称性：理论与实践

由于受保护的方法在流行的编程语言中相当罕见，因此我最近在阅读 Gabriel Scherer 的演示文稿“面向对象/函数式编程对称性：理论与实践”中的幻灯片时发现了它们的存在。

我推荐这个演示文稿，它展示了静态类型函数编程和面向对象编程工具之间的对称性。 尽管这种对称性已被多次观察和研究，但演示文稿是全面且易于理解的（并且相对公正，讨论了两种方法的优缺点）。 不幸的是，在演示过程中没有涵盖（时间通常是演示者的敌人），幻灯片中包含了有关受保护方法的整个部分。 原始示例以经典函数式风格提供了 flatten 函数实现之间的对称观察：

type 'a list = ...
let rec length : 'a list -> int = ...
let rec concat : 'a list -> 'a list -> 'a list = ...

let rec flatten : 'a list list -> 'a list = function
  | [] -> []
  | x::xs -> x @ flatten xs

如果我们在面向对象的世界中，则扁平化方法的实现恰好提出了本说明中介绍的问题。 问题是：flatten 应该有什么类型？

class type ['a] olist = object
  method length : int
  method concat : 'a olist -> 'a olist

  method flatten : ???
end

因此，他提出了这种语法，这意味着对 flatten 方法的保护：

method flatten : 'b olist with 'a = 'b olist

此语法允许描述受保护的方法，并且可以像这样概括：方法 method_name : return_type with generic_type = other_type。 与模块中的替换类似，我们可以使用 and 指定对多个泛型的约束。 例如：方法 foo : string ，其中 'a = string 和 b = int，对于由两种类型参数化的类：class ['a, 'b] t。

此外，这种语法还允许优雅地定义特定的行为。 例如，对于我们的 olist 类型，如果列表的元素是整数，我们可以提供 sum 方法：

class type ['a] olist = object
  method length : int
  method concat : 'a olist -> 'a olist
  method flatten : 'b olist with 'a = 'b olist
  method sum : int with 'a = int
end

所有这些听起来都非同寻常，但不幸的是，这种语法在 OCaml 中不可用。 真烦人！ 别担心，可以使用一些小工具对其进行编码。

OCaml 中的受保护方法

尽管我对用于编码受保护方法的工具有相当清晰的了解，但在遇到一些极端情况后，我决定拜访 OCaml 社区中从不提出问题但总是广泛回答问题的人：Florian Angeletti，也称为 Octachron。 （一个有趣的小提示：octachron 是 MIDI 鼓音序器的名称，所以当我在 Google 上搜索他的昵称时，建议立即包含了 Octachron ocaml）。

我们的目标是允许对某些方法添加约束，以便只有当接收者的类型满足它时才可以访问它们。 在不修改语言语法的情况下，对约束进行建模可以包括提供强制执行它的附加参数。 换句话说，我们要提供证据。

提供类型相等见证

由于在该语言中引入了广义代数数据类型，因此有一种相当简单的方法来定义类型相等见证：

type (_, _) eq =
  | Refl : ('a, 'a) eq

eq 类型只有一个构造函数：Refl，允许表示类型检查器未知的类型相等性。 由于我们只能构造关联两个相等类型的 Refl 值，因此在作用域内实例化 Refl 可以保证这些类型是等效的。 例如：

type other_int = int
let _ : (int, other_int) eq = Refl
(* Now, we have a proof of [int = other_int]. *)

这个例子有些人为，因为这里编译器非常清楚 int = other_int。 但是，在某些情况下编译器无法知道这一点。 例如，当在运行时提供数据时，类型检查器没有关于类型的信息是完全合理的，或者当类型的表示被抽象隐藏时。

本笔记的目的不是深入研究 eq，因此请记住，如果我们可以构造一个 Refl 值，我们就可以保证两个语法不同的类型实际上是相等的。

用 eq 约束

让我们回到为列表提供对象 API 的示例。 这是它的界面：

class type ['a] obj_list =
  object ('self)
    method length : int
    method append : 'a list -> 'a obj_list
    method uncons : ('a * 'self) option
    method flatten : ???
  end

为了给一个扁平化的类型，我们想要强制 'a（obj_list 类的类型参数）是一个列表。 换句话说，我们想要一个证明 'a 属于 'b 列表类型。 也就是说，保证 'a 和 'b 列表虽然语法不同，但相等。 很简单：只需要​​提供 ('a, 'b list) eq 类型的值：

method flatten : ('a, 'b list) eq -> 'b list

现在我们有了一个用 flatten 方法描述列表的接口，该方法将接收者限制为某个列表，让我们具体实现一个实现 obj_list 的类。

实现 obj_list 接口

第一种方法（length、append 和 uncons）很容易实现：

let my_list (list : 'a list) =
  object (self : 'a obj_list)
    val l = list
    method length = List.length l
    method append x = {<l = List.append l x>}
    method uncons = match l with [] -> None | x :: xs -> Some (x, {<l = xs>})

    method flatten = ???
  end

现在，让我们专注于展平。 我们将递归地遍历列表，将每个元素与前一个元素连接起来。 例如，[[1]； [2]； [3]]将变为[1]@[2]； [3]。 除了有些嘈杂的注释之外，整个技巧在于实例化 Refl 以提供 'a = 'b 列表的证据。

method flatten : 'b. ('a, 'b list) eq -> 'b list =
  let rec aux : type a b. a #obj_list -> (a, b list) eq -> b list =
  fun list witness -> match list#uncons with
    | None -> []
    | Some (head_list, xs) ->
        let flatten_list : b list =
          let Refl = witness  in head_list
        in flatten_list @ aux xs witness
  in aux self

添加受保护的方法 sum

现在我们能够限制某些方法，让我们尝试添加一个 sum 方法来生成整数列表的总和！ 首先，让我们将 sum 添加到我们的界面中。 这次，我们想要将类型参数限制为 int。 为此，我们只需将 ('a, int) eq 作为类型相等见证：

class type ['a] obj_list =
  object ('self)
    method length : int
    method append : 'a list -> 'a obj_list
    method uncons : ('a * 'self) option
    method flatten : ('a, 'b list) eq -> 'b list
    method sum : ('a, int) eq -> int
  end

接下来，我们可以实现sum方法，它只是fold_left函数的使用。

method sum : ('a, int) eq -> int =
  let aux : type a. a list -> (a, int) eq -> int = fun list Refl ->
    List.fold_left (fun acc x -> acc + x) 0 list
  in aux l

sum 的实现在逻辑上比 flatten 更简单，因为它没有引入额外的类型变量。 我们可以测试不同的方法：我们可以对 'a list obj_list 类型的对象调用 flatten，对 int obj_list 类型的对象调用 sum。

let a = my_list [ [ 1 ]; [ 2 ]; [ 3 ] ]
let _ = assert ([ 1; 2; 3 ] = a#flatten Refl)
let b = my_list [ 1; 2; 3; 4 ]
let _ = assert (10 = b#sum Refl)

如果我们尝试应用错误类型的受保护方法，例如，尝试对列表 a（其类型为 'a list obj_list）求和，则程序将无法编译。 这是有道理的，因为我们试图在不尊重强加约束的情况下调用受保护的方法。

1 | let _ = a#sum Refl
                  ^^^^
Error: This expression has type (int list, int list) eq
       but an expression was expected of type (int list, int) eq
       Type int list is not compatible with type int

正是预期的行为！ 我们现在可以定义通过类型相等见证来约束接收者类型的方法。 任务完成！

总结一下

令人惊讶的是，受保护的方法并不存在于所有静态类型的 OOP 语言中，因为它们允许表达更多方法，同时保留面向对象编程如此重要的消息传递语义。 我不是面向对象编程语言的大量用户（OCaml 是我唯一经常使用的语言），我不知道有哪些语言为受保护的方法提供语法支持。 然而，我最近了解到，Nicolas Rinaudo 指出，Scala 语言使用类似的编码，但隐式提供类型相等见证，从而减轻了调用，并且不强迫用户手动提供 Refl。

尽管编码有点繁重，并且可以想象本机语言支持可以简化受保护方法的定义，但显式操作类型相等见证允许我们对它们进行编码。 有用吗？ 由于 OCaml 中很少鼓励 OOP 编程，可能不会，但为平等见证人提供一个具体且实用的用例仍然很有趣！
